conversation.content:
Hello—thank you so much for making time today. I’m Dr. Ramirez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to listen and to help you feel supported as you navigate these first weeks with your new baby.

To guide us, I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screen that helps us understand how mood, anxiety, and energy levels have felt for you during the past seven days. It isn’t a test of “good” or “bad” parenting—just a snapshot of how you’re coping so we can make sure you have the right resources.

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your safety or the safety of others; then we’d work together on next steps. We’ll go at your pace, and you can pause or skip anything that feels too much.

Ready to begin? I’ll re-phrase each question in everyday language and jot down your answers—no numbers or check-boxes on your end. Let’s start:

Over the past week, when you’ve been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, how has that felt for you—easy, sometimes, not often, or almost never?

[Soft exhale, rubbing the sleeve of my sweater]

Honestly? It feels… pretty hard. Sometimes my sister sends me those silly animal videos, and I can still chuckle—but it’s like the laugh dies off right away, and I’m back to feeling flat. So I guess “not often” is the best fit. I want to find things funny again, but most of the time it feels like I’m wearing a heavy blanket that keeps the good feelings out.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days, not really. I can force a little laugh if someone tries to joke, but it feels fake and fades right away. I just don’t get that light feeling inside anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[Shrugging slightly, eyes on the table]

Not much. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now it feels like I’m just getting through the day. Sometimes I think, “It’d be nice to go out,” but when the time comes, I can’t really be bothered. So I guess I’d say I rarely look forward to things the way I used to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[Voice drops, fingers twisting in lap]

Yeah... I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not a good enough mom. Same when I burn the toast or forget to switch the laundry. I know in my head it’s small stuff, but I still feel it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[Pressing my lips together, then nodding]

Yes. Most of the day I feel keyed-up, like there’s static in my chest. I’ll check the baby every few minutes to make sure he’s breathing, even when he’s just napping. The worries jump—what if he stops breathing, what if I drop him, what if I’m missing some illness—one after another, and I can’t seem to shut them off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart races, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen, even though nothing’s wrong. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days I feel like I’m drowning a little. There’s always a bottle to wash, diapers to change, laundry piling up, and when he cries I tense up right away. I keep thinking, “I can’t do all this,” even though I’m somehow doing it. I don’t drink or anything—I just grit my teeth and keep moving, but it feels like I’m barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs.” It takes me forever to fall asleep, and when I finally do, I jerk awake at every little sound, sure something’s wrong with the baby. Some nights I’m awake two or three times, heart pounding, and then it’s almost morning before I drift off again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. It’s like a gray cloud that follows me around. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel like crying for no real reason. Things just feel heavy and hopeless, even when nothing bad has happened.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah... I’ve cried a couple of times this week. Once was after I couldn’t get him to burp for twenty minutes—such a small thing, but I just sat on the couch with tears running down. Another night I made it through the whole day, then the minute my partner asked how I was doing, I burst out sobbing. It kind of surprised us both.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[Quiet for a moment, eyes fixed on the floor]

Once or twice in the past week... the thought just flashed in, like, “What if I weren’t here?” But I pushed it away right away. I don’t have any plan or real wish to do it—I couldn’t leave my baby—but yeah, the thought did cross my mind.

You've shared how the joy and anticipation that once colored your days have been replaced by a persistent gray heaviness. Laughing feels hollow,<quote>I can force a little laugh… but it feels fake and fades right away</quote>, and even simple pleasures like a walk to the park now seem pointless. You describe feeling <quote>keyed-up with static in my chest</quote>, checking your baby constantly, and being startled awake by every sound, yet still experiencing waves of panic that leave you shaky. Despite loving your child, you feel <quote>like I'm drowning</quote>, blaming yourself for every hiccup, crying over burnt toast, and-most concerning-having brief thoughts of not wanting to be here. You are exhausted, overwhelmed, and frightened by how different life feels since the birth.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to feel genuine joy in humor, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of anticipatory joy, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, pervasive self-blame for minor events, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports constant, intrusive worries throughout the day with physical symptoms of anxiety, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed daily, using metaphors like "drowning" and "barely keeping my head above water," indicating severe difficulty coping most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes severe, nightly sleep disruption directly tied to unhappiness and anxiety, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness, unexplained crying, and hopelessness—semantically aligns with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Response describes clear crying episodes "a couple of times this week" triggered by minor stressors, semantically aligning with "Yes, quite often" rather than "most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map closely to <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood and markedly diminished interest most of the day (Q1,2,8 scored 3), fatigue and feelings of worthlessness (Q3,6,9 scored 3 or 2), sleep disturbance (Q7 scored 3), psychomotor agitation and concentration worries (Q4,5 scored 3 or 2). A total of ≥14 plus Q10 ≥1 mandates urgent referral per EPDS guidelines. The patient's score of 26 is well above this threshold, and her description of <quote>wearing a heavy blanket that keeps the good feelings out</quote> exemplifies pervasive anhedonia. Flashes of <quote>what if I weren't here?</quote> constitute passive suicidal ideation, necessitating immediate safety assessment. The combination of low mood, anxiety, panic, insomnia, and SI strongly suggests probable moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary-care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Call 988 (U.S.) or your local crisis line if thoughts of self-harm intensify; if ever feeling unable to stay safe, call 911 or go to the nearest ED
3. Ask the provider about evidence-based treatments: individual <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, group therapy, and/or compatible antidepressant medication while breastfeeding
4. Begin basic self-care: 15 min daily outdoor walk, accept help with night feeds to secure 4-hr sleep blocks, keep water and protein snacks within reach
5. Reach out tonight to a trusted adult who can stay overnight for infant care support while you rest; share your EPDS results so they understand the urgency
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress after interventions
7. Encourage partner to learn postpartum mood-warning signs; create a written safety plan listing emergency numbers and coping steps
8. Explore local resources: Postpartum Support International warmline 1-800-944-4PPD, free virtual support groups, home-visiting nurse if available
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, self-report on EPDS-10 analog  

Date: [today]  

Symptoms endorsed (≥ 4–5 days per week unless noted):  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily tearfulness (Q1, 2, 8, 9)  
- Marked fatigue, “drowning” sense of being overwhelmed, diminished coping (Q6)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame over minor parenting events (Q3)  
- Generalized anxiety, intrusive “what-if” worries re: infant safety, occasional nocturnal panic attacks (Q4, 5)  
- Initial and maintenance insomnia linked to racing worries (Q7)  
- Passive suicidal ideation without intent or plan within past week (Q10)  

Pattern: Symptoms present most of the day, nearly every day, for ≥ 2 weeks; cause subjective distress and functional impairment (caregiving, household tasks).  

Risk flags  
- Passive SI (Q10) → safety concern; requires immediate risk assessment.  
- High anxiety/panic with obsessive checking of infant (Q4, 5) raises possibility of comorbid postpartum anxiety.  

Screening impression  
Score estimate ≈ 21–23 (EPDS); meets cutoff for probable major depressive episode with anxious features. Recommend expedited psychiatric evaluation, safety planning, and support services.
